planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring once frost danger has passed, letting the cut end callus for several days before setting it shallowly into a gritty, fast-draining cactus mix in bright, filtered light.

directions: Stapelia leendertziae sends up tall, upright, four-angled stems from a spreading clump and produces some of the darkest flowers in the genus, a deep glossy maroon-black bell shape with recurved lobes and a smooth, almost waxy surface rather than the hairy texture common in related Stapelia species. The blooms carry a strong carrion scent that draws flies for pollination, so it is best sited away from windows or seating areas when flowering. Grow in bright, filtered light with a gritty cactus mix that dries out fully between waterings, and reduce water sharply in winter while keeping the plant above 50 degrees Fahrenheit. Its taller, more erect stems benefit from a slightly deeper pot than mat-forming stapeliads to keep the clump from toppling.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Break off a rooted offset or stem section, let it callus for a day or two, then set it shallowly in a very gritty, fast-draining succulent mix in bright, indirect light; clumps also divide readily.

directions: Huernia barbata forms low mats of soft, toothed stems and is named for the dense fringe of dark, thread-like hairs that lines the edges of its maroon and cream-yellow flowers, giving each bloom a shaggy, bearded outline unlike the smoother-lobed flowers of many related Huernia. The star-shaped blooms open close to the stem base and release a faint carrion odor to attract fly pollinators. Grow in bright, indirect light with brief morning sun, since intense direct exposure can scorch the shallow-rooted stems, and let the gritty mix dry completely between waterings. It is well suited to shallow pots or mixed succulent bowls where its trailing, clustering habit can spread over time.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
University of California Cooperative Extension -- Succulents

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to partial sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix, allowing the soil to dry out fully between waterings.

directions: Orbea lutea is a low, clustering South African succulent with fleshy, four-angled toothed stems that stay smaller and neater than many of its Orbea relatives, making it well suited to shallow dish gardens. Its star-shaped flowers open a clear, glossy yellow marked with fine reddish speckling near the center, a brighter and cleaner color than the mottled maroon-brown blooms typical of the genus, though it shares the same faint carrion scent that draws fly pollinators. Site plants in bright light with some protection from the hottest midday sun, and keep the gritty succulent mix dry between waterings since the shallow roots rot quickly in damp soil. Reduce watering further in winter and protect from temperatures below 50 degrees Fahrenheit.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Break off a rooted offset or short stem section, let the cut end callus for a day or two, then press it shallowly into a very gritty, fast-draining succulent mix in bright light.

directions: Duvalia sulcata forms tight, low mats of small, deeply grooved, finger-like stems that stay closer to the ground than most Stapelia or Huernia relatives, making it a good choice for shallow bowls and rock garden crevices. Its small, dark reddish-brown flowers are thick and fleshy with a slightly reflexed shape, opening flush against the stem clusters and releasing a mild carrion scent for fly pollination. Give it bright light with a little midday shade in hot climates, and use an especially fast-draining, mineral-heavy mix since its congested, shallow stems are prone to rot if kept damp. Water only when the mix is completely dry and withhold water almost entirely through winter.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring after frost danger passes, letting the cut end callus for several days before inserting into a gritty, fast-draining cactus mix in bright light.

directions: Caralluma fimbriata is a clumping Indian succulent with upright, angular, blue-green stems edged in small soft teeth, native to dry scrubland where it grows in gritty, rocky soil under intense sun. Clusters of small maroon-purple flowers with fringed, hair-edged petals appear along the stem edges and carry the mild carrion scent typical of the tribe, though it is noticeably fainter than in many Stapelia species. It tolerates more direct sun than most stapeliads and should be grown in full sun to light shade with an especially lean, fast-draining mineral mix. Water sparingly and only once the soil has dried completely, cutting back further during winter dormancy.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Root short stem cuttings in late spring or summer once temperatures are reliably warm, letting the cut end callus well before inserting into a very lean, fast-draining mineral mix.

directions: Edithcolea grandis is prized among stapeliad collectors for its enormous, intricately patterned flowers, which spread into a five-pointed star marked with a dense mosaic of maroon, cream, and purple resembling a woven carpet, giving the plant its common name. The soft, sprawling stems are more fragile and rot-prone than those of Stapelia or Huernia, so it demands an especially lean, mineral-heavy mix and careful attention to drainage. Grow in bright light with some protection from the harshest midday sun, keep humidity low, and water only when the mix is bone dry, withholding water almost entirely in cool weather. It is best treated as a specimen pot for an experienced succulent grower rather than a casual houseplant.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Sow seed thinly on the surface of a lean, mineral-heavy mix in a warm propagator once temperatures stay reliably above 70 degrees Fahrenheit; seedlings are slow and resent overwatering.

directions: Hoodia gordonii is a spiny, cactus-like stapeliad from the Kalahari region with thick, upright, columnar stems armed with soft-tipped tubercles rather than true spines, and is far more sun and drought tolerant than most of its Stapelia and Huernia relatives. Its pale, saucer-shaped flowers appear near the stem tips and carry a mild carrion scent, though they are far less showy than the flowers of related genera. It needs a very lean, gritty, fast-draining mineral mix and full sun to develop its characteristic dense, upright growth, since low light causes weak, etiolated stems. Water only when the mix is completely dry, and keep it nearly dry through winter, since it is more prone to stem collapse from overwatering than cold.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Break off a rooted offset or short stem section, allow it to callus briefly, then set it shallowly in a very gritty, fast-draining succulent mix in bright light.

directions: Piaranthus geminatus is a small, mat-forming South African succulent with soft, blunt-toothed stems that stay low and dense, similar in scale to a compact Duvalia. Its small star-shaped flowers, often produced in twos near the stem base, are pale yellow to cream with fine reddish speckling and a slightly glossy, fleshy texture, and carry only a faint carrion scent compared with larger-flowered relatives. Grow in bright light with light shade during the hottest part of the day, in an especially fast-draining, mineral-rich mix, since its congested low stems are prone to rot when kept damp. Water sparingly, letting the mix dry completely between waterings, and keep nearly dry in winter.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or offsets in spring after frost danger passes, letting the cut end callus well before inserting into a very lean, fast-draining mineral mix.

directions: Tavaresia barklyi has densely spined, ribbed stems that give it a cactus-like appearance quite different from the smoother, toothed stems of Stapelia or Huernia, an adaptation to its dry, rocky native habitat in southern Africa. Its large, trumpet-shaped flowers spiral outward into narrow, twisted lobes covered in fine hairs, opening pale yellow with maroon speckling and releasing a faint carrion scent to draw fly pollinators. Grow in bright light with some protection from the harshest afternoon sun, in an especially lean, gritty mix, since the soft interior tissue beneath the spines rots quickly if kept wet. Water only when the mix is fully dry and reduce watering sharply through winter dormancy.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
